briefOverview: A father’s urgent warning against sexual temptation using a vivid example of a young man seduced by a promiscuous woman; the chapter contrasts wisdom’s protection with the deadly consequences of folly.
summary: A parental voice exhorts the son to keep and internalize wisdom’s commands so they will protect him from a ‘strange woman’ (v.1–5). The speaker then narrates a scene in which a naive young man, out at dusk, approaches the corner of a woman known for seductive behavior and goes to her house (v.6–13). The woman uses seductive language, claims religious observance and offerings, and describes a richly appointed bed to entice him (v.14–18). Flattered by her words, the young man follows her despite the danger; the narrator compares his path to an ox going to slaughter and a bird to a snare (v.21–23). The chapter closes with a direct admonition to avoid her ways, warning that many have been ruined by her and that her house leads down to Sheol/the chambers of death (v.24–27).
externalContext: Proverbs is part of the biblical Wisdom literature, often framed as father-to-son instruction common in the ancient Near East. The figure of the seductive or foreign woman functions as a stock literary device representing sexual immorality, covenant unfaithfulness, and impulsive folly rather than only a single historical person. Details such as Egyptian linen, myrrh, and cinnamon reflect long-distance trade and signal luxury goods used to portray the woman’s allure. Claims about peace offerings and vows suggest the tactic of using apparent religious observance to mask immoral behavior.
externalReferences: The warning and father–son instruction echo other Proverbs passages that warn against the adulterous or seductive woman, especially Proverbs 1:8–19, Proverbs 5:1–23, and Proverbs 6:20–35. Proverbs 9:13–18 sets the seductress (Dame Folly) against Lady Wisdom, a deliberate literary contrast within the collection. The phrase “apple of thine eye” appears elsewhere (e.g., Deuteronomy 32:10; Psalm 17:8) as an image of cherished protection, linking the opening admonition to broader biblical idiom.
practicalQuestions: How can I make moral teaching ‘stick’ so it becomes an automatic guard in risky situations?
What contemporary forms of flattering persuasion function like the seductress’s speech, and how can I recognize them?
Which practical boundaries or habits reduce the chance of following harmful impulses (time, place, company)?
How should communities address people who use religious language to justify immoral behavior?
uncertainAreas: The identity of the ‘strange woman’ is ambiguous—she may be a literal prostitute, an adulteress, or a personification of folly; the text intentionally uses ambiguous, stock images. Some idioms (e.g., ‘a dart strike through his liver’) and the translation of ‘hell’/‘chambers of death’ (Sheol) carry symbolic force whose precise connotations can vary by translation and historical context.
